title: The publican (Luke 18:9–14)
hook: O God, be merciful to me a sinner, and he went home justified

segments.voice: Yesterday, a widow wore down an unjust judge by never stopping. Your line was don't lose heart. Did you ask again? Day four hundred seventy-five.

Luke tells us who this story is for before he tells it: some people who trusted in themselves as just, and despised others. That's not a description of one group. It's a habit, and it can belong to anybody: the scrolling that ends with at least I'm not like them. Two men go up to the Temple to pray at the same time. One is a Pharisee, careful and devout. The other is a publican, a tax collector, the kind of man the first one looks down on. Today, two prayers.
screen: `WHO THE STORY IS FOR.` → `AT LEAST I'M NOT LIKE THEM.` → `TWO MEN GO UP TO PRAY.`

segments.voice: First the Pharisee. The parable isn't a verdict on Pharisees as a whole, and this one is genuinely devout. He says: "O God, I give thee thanks that I am not as the rest of men", and then the list: not extortioners, unjust, adulterers, nor even like this publican. I fast twice in the week. I give tithes of all that I possess. Those are real practices, and real discipline. The trouble isn't what he does. It's the comparison. He's praying with one eye on God and one eye on the man in the back. Now the publican. He stands far off. He won't even lift his eyes to heaven. He strikes his breast and says eight words: "O God, be merciful to me a sinner." No list. No comparison. No excuses. Just the truth and a request. And Jesus says: "this man went down into his house justified rather than the other." Justified means set right with God. Then the line we heard last week at the dinner table: everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he that humbles himself shall be exalted. The publican's prayer has had a long life. At Mass, during the Confiteor, people strike their breast, an echo of his gesture. And the Catechism links his cry, and the blind man's, to the Jesus Prayer, prayed in the East and the West: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner. Eight words of his, still in use.
screen: `I AM NOT AS THE REST OF MEN.` · `FASTING, TITHING, AND COMPARING.` · `HE STRIKES HIS BREAST.` · `HE WENT HOME JUSTIFIED.` · then, large: `O GOD, BE MERCIFUL TO ME A SINNER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the publican's prayer. Settle, and breathe. Let your eyes lower, the way his did. Notice if your mind starts making a list, either of your good deeds or of other people's faults. Let the list go. If you pray, say his words slowly, in time with your breath: O God, breathing in; be merciful to me a sinner, breathing out. Repeat it, gently, as long as feels right. If you don't pray, simply sit with honesty about yourself, without comparing. The bell holds the time.
The publican. The tax collector at the back of the Temple who prayed eight words without comparing, and went home justified. Today's word.
Your line: be merciful to me. Today, when you catch yourself thinking at least I'm not like them, say the line instead. Day four hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: At the Confiteor near the start of Mass, Catholics strike their breast, and some pray the Jesus Prayer, built in part on the publican's words, slowly with the breath; Eastern Christians may pray it on a prayer rope.

original.note: Greek: be merciful to me, from the word family of atonement and the mercy seat.

trapdoor: what you thought: Pharisees bad, tax collectors good.
what it means: a devout man who despises others and a sinner who simply asks for mercy; the second goes home set right with God.
what a scholar hears: hilaskomai belongs to the atonement word family; the Greek Old Testament calls the ark's cover the hilasterion, the mercy seat.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut uncited claims (tax collector 'working for Rome', neighbors' resentment, fasting and tithes 'beyond what the Law required'); cut the superlative 'one of the shortest prayers there is, and one of the most prayed' and the garbled 'The Catechism names it'; 'It's worth being fair to him' no longer repeats day 466's line; howItsDone no longer says 'many' twice.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 18:11, 18:13 and 18:14.
Jesus Prayer: CCC 2667 gives its common form and 2616 links it to the publican and the blind man; the prayer is quoted as a traditional prayer, not new. Confirm wording.
Fasting twice a week and tithing all income as going beyond the Law's requirements is a common observation; confirm.
Striking the breast during the Confiteor is in the rubrics of the Roman Missal; confirm phrasing 'many Catholics'.
